items.rationale: The order is written into the program, so code moves from extraction to lookup; the model only does the work inside each step. Using a model in a step does not hand it the control flow.

When each result changes what to do next and paths differ per customer, the model must choose the next step in a loop. A fixed order, a single call or a scripted route picked up front cannot adapt mid-way.

items.answer: The code, because the steps are the same every time, so a fixed sequence is cheaper and more predictable.
accepted: code, because the steps never vary
the developer, in code, because the steps are fixed
items.rationale: Known, identical steps need no model-made decisions; a fixed sequence avoids the extra model calls and variability of a loop, which matters on a small budget. An answer that gives the model the ordering shows the learner treats a loop as the default.

Start with the simplest design that could work, here a fixed sequence, and add model-chosen steps only where measured failures show the need. Starting with a loop or several loops pays cost and unpredictability before knowing they are needed.

The ordering failure exists because the model owns the order; code that runs the check first guarantees it. Prompt wording, a larger model or an extra status tool only make the right order more likely, not certain.

Bookings follow the same two steps every time, so code can run them cheaply and reliably; the loop stays where the path really varies. A higher cap, examples or a second loop keep the model in charge of a path that never needed a decision.
